summary: Discusses algorithmic translation between IPv6 and IPv4 addresses using only static configuration. It defines a well-known prefix for such translation and allows networks to use their own prefixes instead.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv4 and IPv6 are like different address styles. This describes a fixed formula for turning one style into the other, using a special agreed starting prefix.

questions: what is the ipv6 well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96
how is an ipv4 address embedded in ipv6
what is an ipv4-embedded ipv6 address
when should i use a network-specific prefix
subtitle: A fixed formula for packing an IPv4 address inside an IPv6 address, and the well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96 for doing it.

tldr.problem: IPv4/IPv6 translators and related gateways such as DNS proxies need to turn an IPv6 address into an IPv4 address and back, using only static configuration and no per-address lookup.
tldr.mechanism: The IPv4 address is embedded in an IPv6 address after a prefix of 32, 40, 48, 56, 64 or 96 bits. The prefix is either the Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96 or a Network-Specific Prefix chosen by the organization.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the address format, translation algorithms and text notation, and gives rules for when each kind of prefix should be used. It updates RFC 4291.

facts.label: Reserved bits
facts.value: Bits 64 to 71 (the u octet) MUST be zero

today: RFC 6052 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4291, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96 is recorded in the IANA IPv6 address space registry.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6052 is part of a series of IPv4/IPv6 translation documents. Other documents specify how translators and gateways behave; this one specifies only how an individual IPv6 address is translated to a corresponding IPv4 address, and the reverse, when an algorithmic mapping is used, meaning one that needs only statically configured information.

The RFC calls anything that derives an IPv4 address from an IPv6 address, or the reverse, an address translator. That covers packet translators and also entities such as name resolution proxies (DNS64) and application layer gateways. Addresses in the resulting format are called IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses: IPv6 addresses in which 32 bits contain an IPv4 address.

The text expects that if encapsulation methods between IPv6 and IPv4 are developed, they will document their own use of this address format.
sections.plainLanguage: Whenever a program needs to turn one kind of address into the other, it follows this one recipe, so everyone gets the same answer.

sections.title: The IPv4-Embedded IPv6 Address Format
sections.content:
An IPv4-embedded IPv6 address is a variable-length prefix, then the 32-bit IPv4 address, then a variable-length suffix. The prefix is either the Well-Known Prefix, 64:ff9b::/96, or a Network-Specific Prefix unique to the organization deploying the translators. Prefix lengths can only be 32, 40, 48, 56, 64 or 96, and the Well-Known Prefix is 96 bits long, so it can only use the last form.

Bits 64 to 71 are reserved for compatibility with the host identifier format in RFC 4291 and MUST be zero. For prefixes shorter than 96 bits, this reserved octet, called u, sits in the middle of the IPv4 address, splitting it. For example, with a /40 prefix 24 bits of the IPv4 address go in positions 40 to 63 and the remaining 8 bits in positions 72 to 79.

The leftover bits form the suffix. They are reserved for future extensions and SHOULD be zero. A translator that receives an address with nonzero suffix bits SHOULD ignore them and proceed as if they were zero. With a /96 prefix there is no suffix.

Two names describe how the format is used. IPv4-converted addresses represent IPv4 nodes inside an IPv6 network. IPv4-translatable addresses are assigned to IPv6 nodes for use with stateless translation.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like an address with a fixed beginning, then the old-style number tucked inside, and spare room at the end that is left blank for now.

sections.title: Translation Algorithms and Text Notation
sections.content:
To build an address, concatenate the prefix, the 32 bits of the IPv4 address and the suffix if needed, to get 128 bits. If the prefix is shorter than 96 bits, insert the null octet u at bits 64 to 71, which pushes the least significant octet out, as in the format table.

To extract the IPv4 address from a /96 prefix, take the last 32 bits. For other lengths, remove the u octet to get a 120-bit sequence, then take the 32 bits that follow the prefix.

Text follows the rules of RFC 4291. Addresses built with the Well-Known Prefix or a /96 Network-Specific Prefix may use the mixed form with dotted decimal at the end. For example, IPv4 address 192.0.2.33 under the Well-Known Prefix is written 64:ff9b::192.0.2.33.
sections.plainLanguage: To go forward you place the old number in its slot. To go back you pick it out of the same slot, skipping the one reserved blank box.

sections.title: Choosing and Using a Prefix
sections.content:
The Well-Known Prefix MUST NOT represent non-global IPv4 addresses, such as the private ranges in RFC 1918, and translators MUST drop packets that combine it with such an address. It SHOULD NOT be used to build IPv4-translatable addresses, because more specific prefixes derived from it cannot be advertised in BGP, so a Network-Specific Prefix SHOULD be used there.

On routing, organizations that advertise the Well-Known Prefix in inter-domain routing MUST be able to provide translation service. Prefixes longer than the Well-Known Prefix MUST NOT be advertised in BGP, since that would import the IPv4 routing table into the IPv6 one, and administrators SHOULD filter them out. Network-Specific Prefixes used for stateless translation MUST be advertised with proper aggregation.

Stateless translation needs no per-flow state. Organizations SHOULD assign a Network-Specific Prefix, and both translatable and converted addresses SHOULD use the same one, so that internal hosts reach each other directly without a trip through the translator. The RFC proposes using no more than 1/256th of an organization's IPv6 allocation: an ISP with a /32 could dedicate a /40, and an end site with a /48 a /56, or possibly a /96 if all translatable addresses are on one link. For its Scenarios 1 and 2 the recommendation is /40 for a /32 and /56 for a /48; for Scenarios 5 and 6 it is /64 or /96.

Stateful translation creates per-flow state. The Well-Known Prefix SHOULD be used, with two exceptions: a Network-Specific Prefix MAY be used for management reasons, and the Well-Known Prefix MUST NOT be used for Scenario 3 (the IPv6 Internet to an IPv4 network), where a Network-Specific Prefix such as a /96 MUST be used. With several translators sharing a prefix, packets of one connection might reach different translators, so use different prefixes per translator or have them coordinate state.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the shared public mailbox address for everyday conversion. Use your own private one when you need to receive visitors directly, and never mix the public one with private home numbers.

sections.title: Why These Design Choices
sections.content:
Two choices are explained: the all-zero suffix and the prefix value. For the suffix, the authors considered checksum neutrality, encoding a port range, and nonzero values. They declined to reserve 16 bits for checksum neutrality because it would not help stateful translation, and neutrality can be reached by choosing a prefix whose one's complement checksum is 0 or 0xffff. A port-range feature, if needed, could use the reserved suffix bits later. With a /32 prefix the zero suffix gives an all-zero interface identifier, which conflicts with the subnet-router anycast address in RFC 4291, but the RFC accepts this because only one node with a translatable address sits in that /64.

For the Well-Known Prefix the options were to reuse the IPv4-mapped prefix ::ffff:0:0/96, to request a /32, or to request a new /96. The mapped prefix was rejected because current Windows and Mac OS versions generate IPv4 packets and not IPv6 packets for it. A /32 was dropped partly because destination-based load balancing does not work with STUN across several stateful translators. A /96 allows dotted decimal at the end of the address, as RFC 4291 requires, and 64:ff9b is checksum neutral because 0064 plus ff9b equals ffff.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors tried a few options and picked the one that already works on today's computers, reads easily in logs, and does not trip up the checking numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Translators are modeled as special routers and share their risks. The RFC adds one risk of its own: spoofing. An attacker could use an IPv4-embedded IPv6 address as the source of malicious packets, which after translation look like IPv4 packets from that source and are hard to trace. The mitigation is reverse path checks, and verifying throughout the network that packets come from an authorized location.

Attackers could also try to make nodes, DNS gateways or translators use wrong prefixes, causing disruption, denial of service and possible information disclosure, so prefixes must be configured securely. Firewalls that filter on IPv4 addresses could be fooled by IPv6 addresses that translate to filtered IPv4 addresses, so traffic to or from embedded addresses should get the same filtering as the embedded IPv4 address. The mechanisms for secure configuration and firewall setup are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a clever sender could write a fake return address in the new style, networks must check that a letter really came from where it claims.

sections.title: IANA Registry Change
sections.content: IANA added a note to the 0000::/8 entry in the Internet Protocol Version 6 Address Space registry. The note states that the Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96, used in an algorithmic mapping between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, is defined out of the 0000::/8 block per RFC 6052.
sections.plainLanguage: The official address book got a new line saying this special range is now reserved for the conversion recipe.
